units.title: Understand the farm's money
units.summary: Separate household and farm money, follow sales and payments, and keep evidence.

lessons.title: Household and farm money
lessons.outcome: Explain why money can enter or leave the farm without being a produce sale or an ordinary production cost.
lessons.reading: Follow what happened. A buyer paid for produce. The owner added some of their own money. The farm borrowed money. All three can put money in the tin, but they are different events. Write the reason beside each amount. When the owner takes money home, record that too. Do not hide it among packaging or transport. The farm and household both matter. Clear records help you see how they support each other.

practice.title: Demonstration
practice.text: Put down the opening-balance card: R1,000. Add C01, the owner's R300 contribution. Count R1,300. Put C01 under “Owner added money”, not “Produce sold”. Remove C02, R120 paid for packaging: R1,180 remains. Add C03, R200 cash sale: R1,380 remains. Point back to the reasons, not only the final total.

practice.title: Guided sorting
practice.text: Give learners C05, C06, C08 and C10 below. Use the headings “Household withdrawal”, “Borrowing”, “Equipment purchase” and “Loan repayment and interest”. Ask which change cash. All four do. Ask whether any is another produce sale. None is. Do not calculate final accounting profit from these headings. Loan principal, interest and equipment need different treatment in full accounts; F6 and F7 develop that distinction.

practice.title: Independent check
practice.text: A grower sells produce for R90 and then takes R30 home. Ask separately: “What was the sale?” and “How much of that cash remains at the farm?” Answers: R90 sale; R60 remains from that receipt. R60 is not the sale value and is not a calculation of profit. Then ask where the R30 should be visible: in the household-withdrawal record.

practice.title: Feedback
practice.text: If the learner reports a R60 sale, place the buyer's R90 payment card beside the R30 withdrawal card. Keep both events visible and ask again. If the learner calls the contribution a sale, ask what produce the owner bought. In this card they bought none.

practice.title: Field task
practice.text: Make headings for farm sales, farm purchases, owner contributions and household withdrawals in a notebook. Use a private record or new practice cards. No personal amounts need to be shared in class.

lessons.title: Cash, sales, amounts owed and profit
lessons.outcome: Follow a credit sale into a later payment without counting it twice, and explain why closing cash is not enough to establish profit.
lessons.reading: A buyer can take produce today and pay later. Record the sale and what the buyer owes. When the payment arrives, match it to that sale. The payment clears the amount owed; it is not a second basket sold. Cash answers how much money is available. Profit needs the income and costs for the period. Some costs or stock information may still be missing. Say what you know and what you still need.

practice.title: Demonstration in three views
practice.text: Make three cards: “Sales”, “Cash tin” and “Buyer owes”. Start after C03, with sales R200, cash R1,380 and nothing owed. Read C04: delivered produce worth R150, buyer pays later. Sales become R350; buyer owes R150; cash stays R1,380. Do not move a cash token. Later, read C07: buyer pays that same R150. Move the owed token to “Settled” and add cash once. Sales remain R350. Keep the invoice reference S02 on both cards so the connection is visible.

practice.title: Guided calculation
practice.text: Work through the event table in order. At the end, sales are R470, cash received from buyers is R350 and buyers still owe R120. Ask the learner to point to S03, which explains that difference. Do not call the R1,380 closing cash profit: it includes opening cash, the owner's contribution and borrowing, and this pack does not supply all production costs, stock or equipment-use information.

practice.title: Independent check
practice.text: A buyer receives produce for R240. They pay R100 now and agree to pay R140 later. Ask for sale value, payment received and amount still owed. Answers: R240, R100 and R140. The current app has paid-in-full/unpaid invoice status, not a partial-payment ledger. Keep this exercise in the workbook; do not mark the full invoice paid or create another sale to force the app to show the balance.

practice.title: Feedback
practice.text: If cash is given as R240, cover the unpaid R140 card and ask what money arrived. If sales are given as R340, place the payment beneath its existing sale instead of adding it as a new sale. Check with a new example, R180 sale and R60 received: R120 remains owed.

practice.title: App companion
practice.text: Read [Make and manage an invoice](https://imbewufield.vercel.app/student/guides/invoices). In the existing sample tour, identify the unpaid/paid-in-full choice and the route for linking an existing sale. Do not enter this entire workbook as crop sales: borrowing and household transfers are different events. The published guide currently teaches text and practice, not a narrated screen recording.

practice.title: Field task
practice.text: Using practice or redacted evidence, connect one sale to its payment. Preserve both dates when they differ. If the payment cannot be found, keep the status unresolved and name the evidence you need.

lessons.title: Keep an evidence trail
lessons.outcome: Reopen a record, locate its supporting reference, and correct a duplicate or wrong unit without inventing a missing value.
lessons.reading: Give each record a date and a clear reason. Keep the receipt, invoice or another useful reference. After saving, open the entry again and compare it with the source. Check the amount and the unit. A kilogram and a bunch are different. If evidence is missing, write what is unknown. Do not use zero to mean ‘I do not know’. Keep a note of a correction so you can explain it later.

practice.title: Demonstration
practice.text: Place S02, “Delivered sale R150 on Day 3”, beside C07, “Payment R150 on Day 6 for S02”. Draw a line between their references. A duplicate card says “New produce sale R150 on Day 6” but shows the same payment reference. Ask what new delivery it proves. None. On the practice worksheet, cross out the duplicate, retain a short correction note and recalculate sales. Do not prescribe deleting real transactions without checking linked invoice behaviour.

practice.title: Guided inspection
practice.text: Give these independent cards: (a) a receipt says 2.5 kg, entry says 2.5 bunches; (b) source says R12.50, entry says R125; (c) transport receipt missing, entry says zero. Learners identify the unit, decimal and missing-evidence errors. Correct (a) and (b) from their sources. For (c), leave the cost unknown until evidence is obtained; a plausible amount is not evidence. These are new error-finding exercises, not additional events in the cash table below.

practice.title: Independent check
practice.text: Hand the learner one correct record and one altered copy. Ask them to find the changed date or unit, identify the source that resolves it, and explain their correction. Then ask them to reopen the saved practice entry. A save message is not enough for this exercise: compare the reopened amount and unit too. A pending sync message is not proof that another device has the entry.

practice.title: Feedback and transfer
practice.text: If a learner can repeat the rule but misses the changed record, simplify to two fields and then reintroduce the date. Success requires finding an error in a fresh example, not reciting “check the receipt”.

practice.title: Field task
practice.text: Build a small evidence folder or envelope, with references that match the notebook. Use sample records if private material cannot be redacted. Keep actual customer details out of classroom screenshots.

shared.title: Facilitation and practice setting
shared.text:
Use a notebook, calculator and the event cards below. Learners may point, sort or explain aloud. Read each card aloud before introducing a table. Do not ask anyone to reveal household income, borrowing, customer details or bank records to a group.

**Every amount below is invented solely for arithmetic practice.** These are neither local prices nor recommended budgets. “Day 1” through “Day 7” are an imaginary week. There is one practice farm, one owner and one cash tin. No bank account, tax, opening debt, opening customer balance, refunds or other cash movements are in this example. The opening R1,000 is counted money already in the tin, not a new sale. The cash result is complete for this deliberately bounded example; its production costs and profit are not complete.

Show each card's reference beside the written entry. All events and amounts are also available in [f1-practice.json](f1-practice.json). The JSON uses whole cents to keep arithmetic exact; learner-facing materials use rand and cents.

shared.title: Shared event cards and answer key
shared.text:
The packaging and transport figures below are payments in the cash exercise. They are not a complete cost-of-production statement. No harvest quantities or crop yields are implied.

| Card | Day | Event and source reference | Cash in | Cash out | Cash after card |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Opening | Before 1 | Counted cash tin | — | — | R1,000.00 |
| C01 | 1 | Owner adds own money; contribution note O01 | R300.00 | — | R1,300.00 |
| C02 | 1 | Pays for packaging; receipt P01 | — | R120.00 | R1,180.00 |
| C03 | 2 | Produce delivered and paid for; S01 | R200.00 | — | R1,380.00 |
| C04 | 3 | Produce delivered on credit; S02 for R150.00 | — | — | R1,380.00 |
| C05 | 4 | Owner takes money home; withdrawal note W01 | — | R80.00 | R1,300.00 |
| C06 | 5 | Loan principal received; agreement L01 | R500.00 | — | R1,800.00 |
| C07 | 6 | Buyer pays the whole S02 balance; payment R02 | R150.00 | — | R1,950.00 |
| C08 | 6 | Equipment bought; receipt E01 | — | R400.00 | R1,550.00 |
| C09 | 7 | Transport paid; receipt T01 | — | R60.00 | R1,490.00 |
| C10 | 7 | L01 payment: R100 principal and R10 interest, per supplied practice statement L02 | — | R110.00 | R1,380.00 |
| C11 | 7 | Produce delivered on credit; S03 for R120.00, still unpaid | — | — | R1,380.00 |

Totals: cash in R1,150; cash out R770; change in cash R380; closing cash R1,380. Produce sales R470, with R350 buyer payments and R120 outstanding. Remaining loan principal R400, based on the supplied R500 borrowing less R100 principal repaid; the R10 interest does not also reduce principal. No interest rate or recommended lending term is implied. Accounting profit remains unknown.

**End-of-unit demonstration:** Give the learner a shuffled copy of these cards. They should restore the order, separate the different reasons for cash movement, connect S02 to R02, identify S03 as unpaid, and explain why profit is unknown. Then use the new partial-payment example to test transfer. Re-teach any missed distinction and assess with different amounts. Do not use a guessed profit figure as the expected answer.

Iowa State University, Your Farm Income Statement

units.title: Keep and reconcile useful records
units.summary: Follow produce and money, reconcile records and explain corrections.

lessons.title: Harvest, stock and destinations
lessons.outcome: Trace one product from opening stock and harvest into its recorded destinations, then compare the calculated remainder with a separate count.
lessons.reading: Start with what was already here. Add what you picked. Record what left and why. A sale, food for home and a gift are different uses. Keep the same unit. At the end, count or weigh what is still here. Compare that with the book. If they differ, look for the cause. A difference is a question to investigate, not proof that someone stole food.

practice.title: Demonstration
practice.text: Put down four counters for opening stock, then add H01's 16 kg. Twenty kilograms are now available. Move six counters to Sold for delivery D01 and two to Home for HOME01. Twelve remain. Read the source reference as you write each row. The sold quantity belongs to sale S01; the home quantity is not another sale or a cash receipt.

practice.title: Guided task
practice.text: Work through Q04–Q08 in the stock table below. Keep each destination in its own column. The book ends with 9 kg. Now uncover the independently supplied count card: 9 kg. Ask which two separate pieces of information agree. Do not claim that agreement proves every record is right; two errors can cancel each other out. Keep the source checks as well as the total check.

practice.title: Independent task
practice.text: Use the worksheet's new 10 kg example. Ask the learner to show 3 kg sold, 2 kg used at home and 4 kg counted at closing. The record explains only 9 kg. One kilogram is unexplained. There is no loss note or second count yet, so “1 kg spoiled” is not a supported answer. Ask what could be checked: a repeat weighing, a missed gift or delivery record, the opening quantity and the units. Do not imply that every difference has the same cause.

practice.title: Feedback
practice.text: If the learner enters bunches as kilograms, hold up the written unit and ask what was actually measured. Weigh a comparable practice bundle or keep its count in a separate record. No conversion is supplied in this pack. If the learner records all remaining produce as home food, point to the crate that is still present. Remaining stock and food already used are different destinations.

practice.title: App companion
practice.text: Read [Record and check a harvest](https://imbewufield.vercel.app/student/guides/harvest). The current form records kilograms and the date of entry, not a backdated picking date. The chart's “kept” is picked minus logged sold quantities; it cannot identify home use, gifts, storage or loss separately. In this workbook, 24 kg picked minus 15 kg delivered is 9 kg; that happens to equal closing stock because the 4 kg opening stock and 4 kg other outflows offset. It is a coincidence, not a general stock formula or an expected app chart result. The current invoice link adds kilogram sale evidence when an invoice is paid in full, so unpaid and partly paid deliveries do not map directly to this workbook. Use its destination records to explain the movement; do not mark an invoice paid just to force the chart to match.

practice.title: Field task
practice.text: Choose one product and a short agreed period. Write the opening amount, unit and how it was measured. Keep source references for additions and destinations. Compare with a separate closing count and list anything unresolved. Do not invent a weight for an unweighed bundle.

lessons.title: Sales, payments and expenses
lessons.outcome: Keep delivery, sale and payment linked; track what a buyer still owes; separate an internal transfer from new farm income or spending.
lessons.reading:
Write the sale when the agreed produce is delivered in this exercise. Keep the payment beside that sale, with the date it arrived. If only some money arrives, show what is still owed. Moving your own money from the cash tin to the wallet does not create another sale. It changes where the money is kept. A fee is a separate payment if the evidence shows one. Keep the amount and cents from the source.”

This exercise's agreed delivery is the point used to record its sale. It is not a rule covering every contract, deposit, return or accounting policy. Those need their own terms and bookkeeping review.

practice.title: Demonstration
practice.text: Read S02: 5 kg delivered on Day 2 for R100.00. Nothing is paid that day. Put R100.00 in “Buyer B owes”. On Day 4, PAY02 shows R60.00 received into the wallet for S02. Move R60.00 out of the owed amount and into wallet receipts; R40.00 remains owed. Sale value stays R100.00 and delivered weight stays 5 kg. The payment has not produced another delivery.

practice.title: Guided transfer
practice.text: Before MOVE01 the cash tin holds R607.50 and the wallet R100.00. Move R100.00 from cash to the wallet. Cash becomes R507.50 and the wallet R200.00. Combined money remains R707.50. Keep both sides connected by MOVE01. This transfer is complete, with no fee attached in the supplied evidence. FEE01 is a separate Day 3 wallet charge of R2.50, not a guessed transfer cost. If a real transfer is pending, record and investigate that state; do not pretend the receiving account already has it.

practice.title: Guided reconciliation
practice.text: Complete all seven money rows. The farm receives R260.00 from buyers and pays R45.00 in documented costs. Combined money changes from R600.00 to R815.00. Sales total R300.00; R40.00 remains owed on S02. Neither R815.00 nor R215.00 is established accounting profit. The pack omits production costs and stock values needed for that conclusion.

practice.title: Independent task
practice.text: A new R90.00 sale has a R30.00 payment. Ask separately for the sale value, money received and amount owed: R90.00, R30.00 and R60.00. Then give the learner a new internal R20.00 transfer between accounts. The transfer alone changes neither total money nor sales. An independently documented R1.00 fee would reduce money by R1.00; it would not make the transfer itself a produce purchase. These are separate practice cases, not extra rows in the main tables.

practice.title: Feedback
practice.text: If the learner adds the transfer to income, move one physical token between the two account mats and ask how many tokens were created. If a part-payment settles the whole sale in their answer, place the R60.00 payment under the R100.00 sale and uncover the R40.00 gap. If cents disappear, compare PACK01's R12.50 with the written entry before recalculating.

practice.title: App companions
practice.text: Use [Record a cost and keep its receipt](https://imbewufield.vercel.app/student/guides/expenses) and [Make and manage an invoice](https://imbewufield.vercel.app/student/guides/invoices). The app currently offers unpaid or paid-in-full invoice status; it does not model the partial-payment or cash-tin/wallet ledgers in this exercise. Keep those in the workbook. Do not mark S02 paid in full, create another sale for its payment, or enter an own-account transfer as a crop sale to make the app resemble the worksheet.

practice.title: Field task
practice.text: Use one approved practice or redacted sale and its payment evidence. Record the separate dates and account, match the reference, calculate any balance and name missing evidence. Do not contact a real buyer as part of this classroom task.

lessons.title: Reconcile the book and correct mistakes
lessons.outcome: Compare independent evidence with records, locate the cause of a difference, and retain a clear correction trail without concealing an unresolved amount.
lessons.reading: Reconcile means compare and explain. Count the cash. Read the wallet statement. Match deliveries, sales, payments and receipts by their references. Check the dates and units as well as the totals. When you find a mistake, keep the original reference and write what changed and why. If you cannot explain a difference yet, say so. Do not add a guessed entry just to make the totals agree.

practice.title: Demonstration
practice.text: The practice book omits FEE01 and reports wallet money of R340.00. The supplied closing wallet statement shows R337.50. Compare the rows, find the R2.50 debit on that statement and add its missing source reference. The book now agrees with the statement. This correction is supported by FEE01, not by a made-up “balancing fee”. If the statement did not show the reason, the difference would remain unresolved.

practice.title: Guided error hunt
practice.text:
Present four altered copies, one at a time. Each begins from the clean main pack; do not stack their errors.

| Altered practice copy | What the learner should find | Evidence-led correction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| H02 is absent; book says only 1 kg remains | Missing 8 kg harvest | Restore H02 from the supplied Day 3 weighing record; closing stock becomes 9 kg |
| PAY02 appears twice; buyer payments total R320.00 | One R60.00 payment counted twice | Retain one payment for its one reference; payments return to R260.00 and S02 still has R40.00 owed |
| MOVE01 is called a new sale | Own money mistaken for revenue | Restore linked transfer treatment; there is no new buyer or delivery supporting a sale |
| PACK01 is written as R125.00 | Decimal error of R112.50 | Copy R12.50 from the source; do not alter the receipt to agree with the entry |

Write a correction note containing the record reference, old entry, corrected entry, source used, date of correction and person checking it. In the paper exercise use a single line through the error so it remains readable. Follow the actual app's supported correction controls for real records; do not prescribe deleting a linked sale or invoice as a routine fix.

practice.title: Independent task
practice.text: The worksheet gives an 8 kg record changed to “8 bunches”, a Day 2 delivery with a Day 4 payment, and a closing count that is still unexplained. The learner must keep the original measurement unit, preserve both event dates and leave the unknown cause unresolved. Being able to repeat the rule does not pass the task; they must find and explain each discrepancy on a fresh copy.

practice.title: Feedback and transfer
practice.text: If the learner changes a source document to fit the total, ask which record was the evidence and which was the copy. If they stop after totals agree, show two offsetting errors: an omitted R5.00 receipt and an omitted R5.00 payment. The net change is zero, but both records are still missing. Ask them to identify the missing events rather than congratulating a balanced total. These two example events are outside the main pack.

practice.title: App practice
practice.text: The published guides provide save/reopen steps for harvests, costs and invoices. Practise through the existing sample tour in the same tab. The sample farm's edited data lives in memory: a full reload restores its starting data, although the tab can remain in sample mode. Reopening within the same session is the task here; sample persistence does not demonstrate real-account sync. On a real account, read pending/offline messages and check the saved result without entering the same event twice. The harvest list currently has no Edit control; keep the exact correction needed rather than inventing an adjustment harvest.

practice.title: Field task
practice.text: Reconcile one small, agreed set of practice records. Mark each source as checked, record the differences, make only supported corrections and leave an unresolved list. Ask for bookkeeping help on treatment that you cannot establish. Do not show account numbers, payment access details or private customer information to the group.

shared.title: Facilitation and practice boundaries
shared.text:
Use the [learner worksheet](f2-worksheet.md) or [four-page printable workbook](../../../../output/pdf/finance-f2-workbook.pdf), a calculator, a notebook and counters representing kilograms and money. Read one event aloud at a time. Let learners point, sort cards, explain aloud or ask someone to write their answer. Introduce the second money account only after the learner can follow the cash tin. Keep real household finances, buyer details and payment credentials out of group exercises and screenshots.

All weights, prices, fees and amounts in this pack are invented for arithmetic practice. They are not local market evidence, recommended fees, budgets or yields. This is a separate four-day practice period for the fictional farm; do not carry forward or add F1's balances. The opening position is given: 4 kg of carrots already stored, R500.00 in a cash tin and R100.00 in a mobile-money wallet, with no buyer balance owed. No field area or production period is supplied, so no yield per area can be calculated.

The exercise tracks the same produce in comparable weighed condition. It excludes purchases, processing, refunds, unknown shrinkage, pending transfers, tax, loans and equipment. In real work, identify additional movements and changes in weighing conditions rather than forcing them into this example. No numerical loss allowance is recommended. Exact quantities are stored as whole grams and money as whole cents in [f2-practice.json](f2-practice.json); the teaching tables use kg and rand.

shared.title: Stock cards and worked answers
shared.text:
All rows describe carrots in kg. Opening stock is from before this exercise; it is not another current-period harvest. “Sold” means the quantity delivered, whether paid yet or not. The independent closing count is 9 kg.

| Card | Day | Reference and event | In kg | Out kg | Stock after card kg |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Opening | Before 1 | Counted opening stock | — | — | 4 |
| Q01 | 1 | H01 harvested | 16 | — | 20 |
| Q02 | 1 | D01 delivered for S01 | — | 6 | 14 |
| Q03 | 1 | HOME01 food used at home | — | 2 | 12 |
| Q04 | 2 | D02 delivered for S02 | — | 5 | 7 |
| Q05 | 2 | GIFT01 given away | — | 1 | 6 |
| Q06 | 3 | H02 harvested | 8 | — | 14 |
| Q07 | 3 | LOSS01 recorded spoilage | — | 1 | 13 |
| Q08 | 3 | D03 delivered for S03 | — | 4 | 9 |

Check: 4 kg opening + 24 kg harvested = 15 kg delivered + 2 kg home use + 1 kg gift + 1 kg recorded loss + 9 kg closing stock. These are quantity records, not money values or a profit calculation.

shared.text:
| Sale | Delivery day | Quantity kg | Agreed value | Payment reference and day | Received | Still owed |

shared.title: Money cards and worked answers
shared.text:
The closing cash count is R477.50 and the closing wallet statement shows R337.50. These observations are supplied separately from the book's running answers. The transfer is already completed; no money is in transit at closing.

| Card | Day | Source and event | Cash tin after card | Wallet after card | Combined after card |
| --- | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Opening | Before 1 | Given starting amounts | R500.00 | R100.00 | R600.00 |
| M01 | 1 | PAY01 received for S01 into cash | R620.00 | R100.00 | R720.00 |
| M02 | 1 | PACK01 packaging paid from cash, R12.50 | R607.50 | R100.00 | R707.50 |
| M03 | 2 | MOVE01, R100.00 cash transferred to wallet | R507.50 | R200.00 | R707.50 |
| M04 | 3 | PAY03 received for S03 into wallet | R507.50 | R280.00 | R787.50 |
| M05 | 3 | FEE01 wallet charge paid, R2.50 | R507.50 | R277.50 | R785.00 |
| M06 | 4 | PAY02 part-payment for S02 into wallet | R507.50 | R337.50 | R845.00 |
| M07 | 4 | TRAVEL01 transport paid from cash, R30.00 | R477.50 | R337.50 | R815.00 |

Combined check: R600.00 opening + R260.00 buyer receipts − R45.00 documented costs = R815.00 closing. MOVE01 contributes zero to this combined change. Cash's R100.00 decrease and wallet's R100.00 increase still appear in their separate records. The R215.00 increase in combined money is not established accounting profit.

shared.title: Assessment and worked feedback
shared.text:
The learner passes the practical task by (a) tracing the 28 kg available into all destinations; (b) matching three sales to payments and retaining S02's R40.00 balance; (c) keeping the internal transfer out of sales and costs; (d) checking cents; and (e) explaining a supported correction and an unresolved difference. Offer a different example after feedback. A guessed zero for missing information or a total that only matches by cancelling errors is not successful reconciliation.

Worksheet answers: stock task 10 − 3 − 2 − 4 = 1 kg unexplained; payment task R90.00 − R30.00 = R60.00 owed; own-account transfer creates no extra combined money; independently documented R1.00 fee reduces it by R1.00. For the altered H02 unit, retain 8 kg from the weighing record. Keep Day 2 as delivery and Day 4 as payment. No evidence supports relabelling the unexplained kilogram as theft, spoilage or a gift.

units.title: Know costs and set prices
units.summary: Include costs, compare prices and test a bounded break-even calculation.

lessons.title: Direct costs, shared costs and family labour
lessons.reading: Start with a product and a period. A direct cost belongs to that product. A shared cost serves more than one product. Use a record of how it was used to divide it, and explain your choice. Divide the cost; do not copy the whole bill into both crops. Keep the family's work hours visible too. No wage paid does not mean no work done. An amount used to value that time is different from cash paid out.

practice.title: Demonstration
practice.text:
Place A01-A04 beneath their own crop headings. A05 is one hire bill for R120.00. The equipment record shows two hours for carrots and four for the second crop: carrots receive 2/6 of the bill, the second crop 4/6. Together the shares must still equal the one bill. A06 is a separate R90.00 market trip. Its agreed practice basis is occupied equal-size crate spaces, two for carrots and one for the other crop. Explain why this bill uses a different record.

There is no universal rule that hours or crate spaces always give the fairest allocation. Ask what caused the shared cost and whether the record describes it. The chosen basis must fit the decision and period. If the usage record is missing, show an unallocated amount and investigate. Do not quietly assign it all to the crop that looks most profitable.

practice.title: Two questions, not two interchangeable labels
practice.text: “Which product uses it?” gives direct or shared. “What changes when this activity changes?” gives fixed or variable. Hiring a tool for an agreed day may be direct to one crop but unchanged if that day's output is a little smaller. Extra packaging may vary with packs sold. A shared bill can contain variable items. Always state the period and the change being considered.

practice.title: Guided practice
practice.text: Allocate both shared bills, add each crop's direct costs and check the combined amount. Then add the separately stated family-time comparison: four hours and six hours at the hypothetical R25.00 per hour. Keep the cash column intact. No payment has been invented, and no family time should be added twice if it is already paid and included elsewhere.

practice.title: Independent attempt
practice.text: A new R75.00 hire bill was used one hour by one activity and two hours by another. Divide it and check the sum. Then explain why “shared” does not automatically mean “fixed”. Classify an owner withdrawal and an equipment purchase separately; neither should be hidden inside materials used. Equipment use and its cash purchase may fall in different periods; ask for bookkeeping help on the appropriate treatment.

practice.title: Feedback
practice.text: If both crops receive R120.00, place the single hire receipt between them and ask how the farm obtained two bills. If the learner divides every shared cost equally, ask which source supports the equal split. If family time becomes a cash payment, ask for the payment evidence. Retry with the new hire bill rather than repeating the original numbers.

practice.title: App connection
practice.text: Use the published [expense guide](https://imbewufield.vercel.app/student/guides/expenses) to record an actual paid cost and find its receipt in the sample workflow. Use this workbook for the allocation exercise. Do not create a second expense merely to assign one existing bill to another crop, or enter an unpaid comparison value as money spent. The app's current records are not proof that every cost has been included.

practice.title: Field task
practice.text: Choose one small practice enterprise. Name its product, unit and period. Collect three redacted cost references, identify a shared cost and record a possible allocation basis. List missing evidence. Do not require learners to disclose private household finances.

lessons.title: Unit cost, contribution and break-even
lessons.reading: A cost per unit needs two things: the costs you included and the quantity you divided by. Say both. Produce available for sale is not always produce sold. A selling price may cover some costs and still leave others unpaid. Contribution is what remains after the included variable costs. It must still cover fixed costs. A break-even answer is useful only when its assumptions fit and the required sales can be achieved.

practice.title: Demonstration A - choose the denominator
practice.text:
The carrot exercise has R220.00 of assigned paid costs and 40 kg of marketable produce. That is R5.50 per marketable kg for those included costs. With the separate R100.00 family-time comparison, the total becomes R320.00, or R8.00 per marketable kg. These are two labelled views of one budget, not two bills to add.

If only 32 kg is expected to sell, recovering that same R320.00 entirely through those sales requires R10.00 per kg sold. This is a **sales-recovery planning target**, not the accounting cost of each item sold or a promise that a buyer will pay it. The other 8 kg is not automatically lost or household food; investigate its destination and value. Do not write off closing stock simply because it has not sold. Missing land, equipment, administration, finance and tax information means full profit is still unknown.

practice.title: Demonstration B - a separate simplified model
practice.text:
B01 supplies included fixed costs of R105.00 per practice cycle and variable costs of R7.50 per pack. Each pack is 1 kg and sells for R12.00. For this model only, every pack prepared is sold, price and variable cost stay constant, and fixed costs stay unchanged up to the stated capacity of 30 packs. It is not a forecast derived from the carrot harvest.

Contribution per pack is R12.00 minus R7.50 = R4.50. R105.00 divided by R4.50 is 23 and one-third packs. Whole packs require rounding **up** to 24. Verify on either side: at 23 packs the model is R1.50 short; at 24 it has R3.00 left after its included costs. Call that the model surplus, not full farm profit. This model does not account for prepared-but-unsold packs, waste, changing rates, bad debts or omitted costs. A real plan with those features needs them added explicitly.

practice.title: Guided practice
practice.text:
At 30 packs, calculate revenue and both kinds of included cost. Repeat for 18 packs prepared and sold. Then keep the original prices but reduce capacity to 20. The numerical break-even point does not change, but it is outside that capacity. Never recommend “sell more” without testing production capacity and evidence of demand. Expected sales are assumptions, not confirmed orders.

If price equals or is below variable cost while fixed costs remain positive, more units do not cover those fixed costs under this model. Report no feasible break-even quantity under these assumptions, not zero units. If a cost is missing, the result is unknown; an empty value is not a free input.

practice.title: Markup and margin
practice.text: A separate card gives included cost R8.00 and selling price R10.00. The difference is R2.00. As a share of cost it is 25% markup; as a share of selling price it is 20% margin on those included costs. These are different denominators. Neither is a complete net-profit margin if costs are missing.

practice.title: Independent attempt
practice.text: Use fixed costs R80.00, price R10.00, variable cost R6.00, and capacity 18 whole packs. Find the break-even quantity and explain the capacity problem. Then compare a R6.00 included cost with a R7.50 selling price: calculate markup and margin, naming the denominator each time.

practice.title: Feedback
practice.text: For an answer of 23 packs, ask the learner to multiply 23 by R4.50 and compare with R105.00. For “25% margin”, ask “25% of which amount?” For a missing variable cost treated as zero, restore the blank source card and ask what evidence is missing. For “profit”, have the learner name an excluded cost and relabel the result.

practice.title: App connection
practice.text: Keep these what-if calculations in the workbook. Do not enter forecast sales as actual sales in My Records. Use the existing expense and harvest guides to find the underlying real records. A chart based on saved rows does not supply a missing stock valuation, family-time value or depreciation policy.

practice.title: Field task
practice.text: Prepare one labelled cost-per-unit estimate from agreed practice data. Write the period, costs included, exclusions, unit, expected quantity sold, and source date. Test a smaller sales quantity. Explain what evidence is needed before using the estimate to negotiate a real price.

lessons.title: Compare buyers and agree a price
lessons.reading: Compare the whole offer. Check the weight, quality, price, packaging, delivery and payment date. Use the same unit for both buyers. A higher price can leave less after delivery. Money promised for next week is not money available today. Write down what is agreed, and check what is still unknown before choosing.

practice.title: Demonstration
practice.text:
Decision C offers the same 20 kg of accepted produce to either Buyer A or Buyer B. A offers R10.00/kg, collects it, requires no extra packaging and pays on Day 0. B offers R12.00/kg, but the grower pays R35.00 delivery and R10.00 additional packaging; B promises payment on Day 7. These are alternatives, not two simultaneous sales of the same produce.

A leaves R200.00 after the specified offer-specific cash costs. B leaves R195.00. A's lower headline price leaves R5.00 more at that stage. Both options also relate to R140.00 of already-incurred common costs; subtracting those gives R60.00 and R55.00, respectively. Those are partial results, not full profit. Do not charge the common cost twice or add the two offers together.

The cards separately record additional unpaid selling work: half an hour for A, one and a half for B. At the same hypothetical comparison value, that adds R12.50 or R37.50 to the management view, leaving R47.50 or R17.50 after the specified common costs and additional family-time value. The farm has not paid those wages. Other omitted work or costs could still change the full result.

practice.title: Guided decision
practice.text: State what the supplied evidence favours: A retains more after these specified costs, requires less additional time and pays earlier. Do not claim the buyer is reliable merely because the card promises payment. Ask about confirmed quantities, acceptance standards, rejections, collection arrangements and how the agreement will be recorded. A real buyer relationship may have advantages the cards do not describe; name those separately rather than inventing a monetary score.

practice.title: Independent attempt
practice.text: For a fresh 10 kg, a collecting buyer offers R10.00/kg and a delivery buyer R12.00/kg. The delivery charge is missing. Find the charge at which their cash results would be equal, and explain why no final ranking is justified yet. Another buyer quotes per crate without a crate weight: explain what measurement is needed before comparing it with a per-kg price.

practice.title: Feedback
practice.text: If the learner chooses B just because 12 is greater than 10, lay the delivery and packaging cards beside that offer. If Day 7 money is treated as today's cash, move its payment card along a paper calendar. If the missing delivery charge becomes zero, keep the result blank and write the next question to ask.

practice.title: App connection
practice.text: The [invoice guide](https://imbewufield.vercel.app/student/guides/invoices) covers checking the buyer, units, amounts and payment status after an agreement. An invoice is not evidence that payment arrived. Link an existing recorded sale rather than recording it again. These alternative quotes belong in the workbook; do not create two sample sales and present both as completed business. Partial payments still need a separate balance record; do not mark an invoice paid in full after a deposit.

practice.title: Field task
practice.text: Obtain two redacted or facilitator-supplied offers for a clearly specified product. Record the quote date and all conditions. Compare the supported costs and payment timing. Give a reasoned choice or say precisely which missing fact prevents one.

shared.title: Before teaching
shared.text:
Bring paper, a calculator and the learner workbook. Read the cards aloud if needed. Learners may point, sort cards or explain their answer to a partner; fluent reading is not the assessment. Begin by asking what it costs to get one product from the garden into a buyer's hands. Keep quantities, time and money on separate lines.

All amounts, weights, work hours and quotes below are **invented classroom inputs**. They are not recommended prices, wages, productivity rates or yields. The R25.00 hourly value is a comparison assumption, not a legal wage or payment instruction. No area, real growing season or tax status is supplied. Do not infer these. A, B and C are separate exercises; do not add their totals or carry forward F1/F2 balances.

Outcomes: assign a cost once; explain the basis for sharing it; keep unpaid work visible; use the right denominator; distinguish markup from margin; test a bounded break-even calculation; and compare buyer terms without equating the highest price with the best outcome.

shared.title: A - Worked allocation and cost-per-unit answers
shared.text:
The second crop is deliberately unnamed. Only carrots have a supplied marketable quantity, so the second crop's unit cost cannot be calculated.

| Card | Source | Carrots | Second crop | Combined |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| A01 | Carrot materials used | R96.00 | R0.00 | R96.00 |
| A02 | Carrot packaging used | R24.00 | R0.00 | R24.00 |
| A03 | Second-crop materials used | R0.00 | R144.00 | R144.00 |
| A04 | Second-crop packaging used | R0.00 | R36.00 | R36.00 |
| A05 | R120.00 hire; recorded hours 2 and 4 | R40.00 | R80.00 | R120.00 |
| A06 | R90.00 trip; equal-size crate spaces 2 and 1 | R60.00 | R30.00 | R90.00 |
| CASH | Assigned paid costs | R220.00 | R290.00 | R510.00 |

| VIEW | Included costs plus family-time comparison | R320.00 | R440.00 | R760.00 |

| A08 | R8.00 | R320.00 / 40 marketable kg; includes family-time comparison |
| A09 | R10.00 | R320.00 / 32 expected kg sold; recovery target for included costs |

The zero entries above mean the supplied direct card belongs wholly to the other crop. They do not mean all other costs are known to be zero. Full profit remains unknown.

shared.title: B - Worked break-even and percentage answers
shared.text:
Each case starts from B01 and applies only its stated change.

| Case | Change | Contribution per pack | Whole-pack break-even | Within capacity? | Result at stated sales |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | --- | ---: |
| B01 | Base; capacity and sales 30 | R4.50 | 24 | Yes | R30.00 |
| B02 | Only 18 prepared and sold | R4.50 | 24 | Yes; demand still matters | -R24.00 |
| B03 | Capacity and sales 20 | R4.50 | 24 | No | -R15.00 |
| B04 | Price R7.50 | R0.00 | None | No | -R105.00 |
| B05 | Price R7.00 | -R0.50 | None | No | -R120.00 |
| B06 | Variable cost missing | Unknown | Unknown | Unknown | Unknown |

At 23 packs B01 is **-R1.50**; at 24 it is **R3.00**. A break-even quantity below capacity is not proof of demand. B04/B05 have positive fixed costs and no positive unit contribution; B06 lacks required evidence.

| Card | Included cost | Selling price | Difference | Markup on cost | Margin on selling price |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| M01 | R8.00 | R10.00 | R2.00 | 25% | 20% |

shared.title: C - Worked buyer comparison
shared.text:
| Offer | Agreed sales value | Extra delivery and packaging | After those cash costs | After common R140.00 | Additional time value | After that time value | Payment promised |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| C01 | R200.00 | R0.00 | R200.00 | R60.00 | R12.50 | R47.50 | Day 0 |
| C02 | R240.00 | R45.00 | R195.00 | R55.00 | R37.50 | R17.50 | Day 7 |

These are alternative offers and partial management results, not money already received or full net profit. The additional family hours relate only to this selling decision; they are not the hours from A.

shared.title: Independent answers and assessment
shared.text:
The new R75.00 hire allocation is **R25.00 and R50.00**. The new break-even case needs **20 packs**, beyond capacity 18; at 18 its model result is **-R8.00**. R6.00 cost and R7.50 price give **R1.50 difference, 25% markup and 20% margin**. The fresh buyer comparison gives collection value R100.00 versus delivery value R120.00 before the unknown charge: the cash results tie at **R20.00 delivery cost**. Below that charge the delivery offer retains more; above it collection retains more, considering only these stated cash items. With the charge missing, no final ranking follows.

To pass, the learner must allocate each bill once, check the total, name the basis, keep time value separate from cash, use and label a correct denominator, round whole-unit break-even upward, reject a capacity or evidence gap, and compare an offer beyond its price. One correct total with an incorrect explanation is insufficient. Supply a fresh case after feedback; record what the learner actually demonstrates. Completion is evidence of these practice skills, not certification of a business's profitability.

units.title: Budget and manage cash through the season
units.summary: Build a budget, put money on dates and investigate a cash gap.

lessons.title: Build an enterprise and whole-farm budget
lessons.outcome: Combine two activity budgets without counting shared bills twice, distinguish cash spending from unpaid resource use, and identify missing costs and capacity evidence.
lessons.reading: A budget is a plan with reasons behind the numbers. Name the activity and the period. Show what you expect to sell and what you expect to use. Keep shared bills once in the farm total. Family work still matters when no wage is paid. Write down what you do not yet know. A positive answer on paper does not prove that the land, water, time or buyers are available.

practice.title: Demonstration
practice.text:
The source cards give expected sales of R600.00 for A and R500.00 for B. Direct inputs are R220.00 and R180.00. Share the R120.00 hire using recorded planned hours, two for A and four for B. Share the R90.00 trip using two and one equal-size crate spaces. A receives R40.00 hire and R60.00 trip; B receives R80.00 and R30.00. Combined shared allocations remain R210.00, not R420.00.

The budget's specified cash inputs total R610.00. Separately show four and six hours of unpaid family work at the exercise comparison value of R25.00/hour, giving R250.00. That rate is a hypothetical comparison, not a wage recommendation or assertion of outside earning opportunities. After these included costs the two activities show R240.00 in planned surplus. Land, owned-equipment use, administration, finance costs, tax and other missing costs prevent this from establishing full farm profit. Do not add the time comparison to the cash payments.

practice.title: Guided practice
practice.text: Build the A and B columns and reconcile their sum to the original shared bills. Explain why paying R250.00 for equipment in March is a cash movement but does not establish a R250.00 cost of equipment use for this activity period. The value of its use and accounting treatment need separate evidence and bookkeeping review. Household withdrawal is also a cash movement, not automatically a crop input.

practice.title: Capacity discussion
practice.text: A whole-farm plan also needs the actual availability and timing of land, water, labour, tools and markets. Two activities cannot each be assigned all of the same scarce resource at the same time. This pack supplies cost-sharing hours, not proof that a particular tool or worker is available on the required dates. Keep those checks unresolved until evidence exists. Do not invent a yield from the sales value.

practice.title: Independent attempt
practice.text: A new shared R60.00 bill is divided by recorded use of one unit and two units. Allocate it, then check the total. A learner says a R500.00 funding application makes the two activities profitable: ask them to identify approval, cash receipt and whether funding is a sale. Do not assume it is a grant or loan when the terms are absent.

practice.title: Feedback
practice.text: If the farm total includes both the shared bill and its allocations, physically remove the duplicate card. If unpaid family time becomes a cash payment, ask for payment evidence. If a missing cost becomes zero, replace the zero with an unresolved source request. Give a fresh allocation after feedback.

practice.title: App connection and field task
practice.text: The [expense companion](https://imbewufield.vercel.app/student/guides/expenses) helps find actual recorded costs. It does not create this forecast. Keep the proposed budget in the workbook, label actual evidence and estimates, and give each estimate a source date. Bring one redacted quote and one capacity question for local review.

lessons.title: Put receipts and payments on their dates
lessons.outcome: Calculate a dated cash projection, carry closing balances forward, and detect a shortfall hidden by a positive month-end balance.
lessons.reading: Start with money that is available at the beginning. Add a receipt when you expect the money to arrive. Subtract a payment when it must leave. Carry the balance to the next date. An invoice is not cash received. Check the dates between month ends too. A good total at the end cannot pay a bill that comes before the money arrives.

practice.title: Demonstration
practice.text:
Start at R300.00. Pay the planned R220.00 on 5 January: R80.00 remains. The next planned R180.00 payment on 10 January produces a projected minus R100.00. Stop the cards here and ask how that payment could be made. No borrowing facility or extra money has been supplied. Continue the calculation as a clearly labelled unfunded projection, not as an instruction to pay unavailable cash. The R120.00 hire on 20 January takes it to minus R220.00; the R600.00 receipt on 25 January brings it to R380.00.

The first shortage is 10 January and the deepest base-case shortage is R220.00 after the 20 January payment. January nevertheless closes at positive R380.00. A monthly closing-only check misses the earlier gap. If a receipt and payment share a real date, check which clears first; this exercise avoids same-date ambiguity. Combined available funds also do not prove the right payment account has accessible funds at the required moment.

practice.title: Guided practice
practice.text:
Continue through February and March. Opening balance plus receipts minus payments equals closing balance. February opens with January's R380.00, not the original R300.00. March's R120.00 collection concerns a customer balance from before the exercise; it is a cash receipt now, not another current-season sale. Paying the old R80.00 supplier bill also needs cash now even though it is not one of these current activity inputs.

Set aside X01, the R50.00 transfer from bank to cash tin: both are already inside the combined cash scope, and the supplied transfer has no fee. It changes location, not the combined amount. Set aside X02, the unapproved R500.00 application. Keep the two issued invoices X03/X04 as links to expected buyer receipts; do not count each invoice and its eventual receipt as two inflows. Family-time comparison is not a payment either.

practice.title: Independent attempt
practice.text: In a separate example, open with R90.00; pay R130.00 on Day 2, receive R80.00 on Day 10 and pay R20.00 on Day 20. Find closing cash, lowest projected cash and the first date requiring a response. Then ask whether the closing answer is complete if an additional payment fee is known to apply but its amount is missing.

practice.title: Feedback
practice.text: For a learner who subtracts the net inflow, use counters: opening R10.00, receipt R5.00 and payment R3.00 leaves R12.00. For a learner who sees only the positive ending, replay one card at a time and stop at the first negative projection. For an invoice counted as cash, place its promised receipt on the later date. Ask for a new dated example after correction.

practice.title: App connection and field task
practice.text: The live records/chart series summarises recorded events and has its own payment and missing-data boundaries. It is not this dated forecast or an available-bank-balance guarantee. Keep invented examples and future expected receipts out of actual My Records. Use the [invoice companion](https://imbewufield.vercel.app/student/guides/invoices) to check an existing unpaid invoice and its source, without marking it paid to make the plan balance. Build a short redacted forecast with exact dates; reconcile its opening funds and list restrictions or timing uncertainty.

lessons.title: Test changes and make a reasoned response
lessons.outcome: Change timing, amounts and uncertainty separately, identify combined stress, and explain a response that is feasible before the first shortfall.
lessons.reading: Ask what changes if the buyer pays late, less produce sells, or an input costs more. Change the matching card and recalculate from that point onward. A delay changes when cash arrives. A lower sale changes how much arrives. Test them together too. Write down the evidence needed for your response, and check the plan again before committing.

practice.title: Demonstration
practice.text:
In LATE, move only A's R600.00 receipt from 25 January to 28 February. Do not make a new receipt or change the sale value. The March closing remains R430.00, but the deepest gap grows from R220.00 to R310.00, after the 5 February trip payment. Equal end totals do not imply equal ability to pay on time.

In HIGH, increase B's input payment from R180.00 to R240.00, with no other change. In COMBINED, apply this increase and the late A receipt together. Do not add the individual scenario balances together: each scenario starts from the same opening position and recomputes the changed events. The combined deepest gap is R370.00 and the closing balance is R370.00.

practice.title: Guided practice
practice.text: LOW reduces B's expected sales and receipt from R500.00 to R350.00; this is a lower-sales case, not a claim that a R500.00 debt has been settled in full. OUTSIDE moves B's same R500.00 receipt to 20 April, beyond the 31 March horizon. It remains an expected amount owed, not vanished money; exclude it from cash received inside the horizon. UNKNOWN removes B's input quote. Later exact balances and the deepest gap become unknown, not larger positive balances caused by treating a blank as free.

practice.title: Compare responses
practice.text: DEFER moves the proposed R250.00 equipment purchase to 10 April, assuming the purchase date can actually be changed by agreement. It improves the March closing figure to R680.00 but leaves January's R220.00 gap. It therefore does not solve that earlier problem. A response must work before the shortage: possible options to investigate include changing the scale and associated costs/revenue, agreeing timing with the buyer or supplier, or identifying genuinely available funds. Do not simply delete essential inputs, assume a buyer pays early, cut basic household needs, or treat an unapproved application as available cash. Borrowing requires its full terms and a repayment plan; this unit recommends no lender or loan size.

practice.title: Independent decision
practice.text: Give the learner LATE and DEFER without the answer table. Ask which date first fails, whether the proposed equipment deferral solves it, and what evidence would be needed for a different response. Then present a real unknown quote: accept “cannot calculate yet” with a precise source request. Do not reward a guessed zero for producing a tidy budget.

practice.title: Feedback and field task
practice.text: A good response names the affected date and amount, what can actually change, what must be agreed, and the consequences for later costs, production and receipts. After corrective feedback, use fresh dates or values. For a redacted local practice plan, keep base and adverse cases side by side, label assumptions and set a review date. Compare actual evidence with the plan when it arrives; retain the original forecast rather than rewriting it to pretend it predicted the outcome.

shared.title: Prepare the session
shared.text:
Bring a calculator, paper, date cards and counters. Read one card aloud at a time. Learners may point, move cards, explain aloud or ask a partner to write. Use the timeline for demonstration, then hide its answers for independent practice. Do not require anyone to share private household accounts, customer names or bank details.

All dates, amounts, working hours and offers are **invented classroom inputs**. January-March 2027 is a practice horizon, not a recommended South African growing season. Activities A and B have no specified crop, area or yield. Do not infer one. This is a new exercise, not a continuation of F1-F3 balances. The opening cash tin has R120.00 and the bank R180.00, both assumed available, with no restrictions or fees in the supplied model. The separate opening amounts owed are R120.00 by a customer and R80.00 to a supplier. Neither is opening cash.

A negative projected balance means the proposed sequence cannot be paid from the specified available funds. It is a warning to revise the plan or establish an appropriate, evidenced funding arrangement. It is not cash that exists, an approved overdraft or permission to miss a bill. Later balances describe an **unfunded projection**, not evidence that the intervening transactions could happen. Exact shortfall amounts are model results, not recommended loans or contingency reserves.

shared.text:

units.title: Sell, invoice and collect payment
units.summary: Connect orders, deliveries, invoices and payments without duplicate sales.

lessons.title: Follow the order, delivery, invoice and receipt
lessons.outcome: Explain what each document proves, preserve the quantity and unit, and distinguish a sale from cash collected against it.
lessons.reading: Keep the story of one sale together. First, agree what the buyer wants and how payment will work. Check what you deliver. Check the invoice against that delivery and the agreed price. When money arrives, match it to the same invoice. The payment does not create another basket of produce. Keep its date and reference so you can show what is still owed.

practice.title: Demonstration
practice.text:
Lay out P01: Day 1 order O01 for R120.00; Day 2 completed delivery and invoice D01-I01 for R120.00; Day 3 receipt R01-A for R40.00. Invoice value is R120.00, money received is R40.00, and the recorded balance is R80.00. On Day 4 the buyer asks for another copy. I01-COPY is the same invoice, not another R120.00 sale. On Day 5 receipt R01-B adds R80.00. Total collected is now R120.00 and the balance is zero. Do not add the order, invoice, copy and receipts together as revenue.

Use the app companion's four-stage payment example to reveal one stage at a time. Pause before each answer. The animation is an explanation using invented numbers, not a live account or a demonstration that the app supports part-payment allocation.

practice.title: Guided practice
practice.text: Invoice M01 has two lines: 2.5 kg at R12.00/kg and three bunches at R8.00/bunch. Calculate each line, then add money. The result is R54.00. Do not add the quantities as 5.5 kg. A bunch has no supplied mass. If a line lacks a price or unit, stop and resolve that source instead of choosing a convenient zero or conversion.

practice.title: Independent attempt
practice.text: Give the learner four new blank document cards. Read aloud: an agreement is made, produce is delivered, an invoice is issued, and a buyer pays only some of it later. Ask the learner to place each card in the correct sequence and identify the evidence still needed. Then supply the independent R150.00 invoice and R50.00 receipt. Ask for the recorded amount still owed and what would prove settlement.

practice.title: Feedback
practice.text: If invoice value becomes cash received, move the unpaid portion into the “customer owes” envelope. If a copy creates new income, place it behind the original invoice instead of beside a second basket. If mixed quantities become kilograms, return to the two labelled lines. Give a fresh example after feedback.

practice.title: App connection and field task
practice.text: Use [Record a sale once](https://imbewufield.vercel.app/student/guides/sales). Before any real entry, find the matching existing sale or invoice. Collect a redacted set of order, delivery, invoice and receipt references and explain any gap. This lesson does not require sending a customer message or sharing private documents.

lessons.title: Choose the right invoice route and verify the saved result
lessons.outcome: Choose new, past or paper entry appropriately; preserve a source reference; reopen or link an existing sale; and check the saved result without creating duplicate income.
lessons.reading: Look in your records before you add anything. If the invoice is already there, open it. If the sale is there but needs an invoice, use that sale. If you are bringing in an older or paper record, keep its original reference and dates. Read the save message. Open the saved document and check it. A second copy of a document must not become a second sale.

practice.title: Demonstration on the actual app
practice.text:
Start in the sample tour, confirm it is sample data, and open My Records → Sold. Show New sale & invoice and Past sale / paper invoice. Show View invoice for an already linked sale and Create invoice when an eligible existing sale needs one. Reopening is different from starting a blank form.

Choose Invoice type and, when asked, Existing sale record **before** entering buyer and line details. Changing either starts a fresh form in the current app. A new invoice begins a new document. Produce already sold and An invoice already written on paper ask whether the sale exists. Select the source sale when applicable; do not choose No merely to avoid matching it. An already invoiced sale should be reopened, not invoiced again. Preserve the original paper reference when the paper route asks for it.

Check buyer, product, quantity, unit, agreed price, growing area where relevant, dates and payment status. A suggested price is not evidence of the buyer's agreement. Keep bags and bunches as their actual units. The app can link paid kilogram lines into crop-sale evidence; it cannot infer the mass of other units. Existing-sale linking is limited by the supported source records. Do not split one past sale into invented new sales to make the form accept it.

Save, read the actual message, and reopen the same invoice from Saved or its sale link. Check its number, total, date and status. A device save with crop-sale synchronisation pending is not a reason to create another invoice. Documents are currently saved on the device within the account scope; crop-sale sync does not prove the complete invoice document is available on another device.

practice.title: Guided practice
practice.text:
Sort these situations: (a) an invoice already saved; (b) an eligible sale already recorded with no invoice; (c) a completed sale not yet recorded; (d) an old paper invoice whose sale may already exist. Explain the lookup step and route for each. For (d), missing evidence about an existing sale stays unresolved until checked. “Paper” does not mean “unpaid”.

Use the prepared sample invoice to demonstrate unpaid → paid in full only when the exercise supplies full payment evidence. Keep the same invoice identity. A receipt date and invoice issue date answer different questions. The current app gives the whole paid invoice one receipt date in its records/chart series. For instalments on different dates, the separate supporting schedule must retain each actual receipt date; the app chart cannot represent that full cash history. If the app does not support the original record faithfully, retain it separately and identify the limitation instead of manufacturing a replacement history.

practice.title: Independent attempt
practice.text: Present a saved R150.00 invoice and the R50.00 receipt from F5.1. Ask whether to create a second R50.00 sale, mark the original paid in full, or keep the part payment in a separate checked balance record. Only the last fits these facts. Then ask what to inspect before downloading a requested copy of the existing invoice.

practice.title: Feedback and field task
practice.text: For duplicates, start at the existing reference and follow it to the document. For premature full payment, compare the invoice amount with all verified receipts. For altered dates, return to original evidence. In the sample workspace, reopen one prepared invoice and identify its amount, payment status and source. Print/PDF is a separate document check; downloading does not send it to a customer. Use the [invoice companion](https://imbewufield.vercel.app/student/guides/invoices) for the detailed steps.

lessons.title: Reconcile deposits, part payments and unresolved balances
lessons.outcome: Keep cash receipts, allocations, adjustments and questions distinct; explain a remaining balance; and know when the current app needs a separate supporting schedule.
lessons.reading: Write down every payment once, with its evidence. A deposit may arrive before produce is delivered. Keep it linked to that customer and order. Later, applying that same deposit to an invoice does not bring in more money. Keep questions and agreed corrections visible. If money arrives and you do not know who sent it, investigate before matching it to a sale.

practice.title: Deposit demonstration P02
practice.text:
Day 1 order O02 is R90.00. Day 2 advance DEP02 is R30.00; nothing has been delivered and no invoice issued in this exercise. Cash received is R30.00 and the customer's advance remains separately held in the record. This describes an outstanding obligation, not a promise that a separate physical bank account exists. It does not establish completed sales revenue.

Day 5 completed delivery and invoice D02-I02 is R90.00. First identify the original R30.00 receipt, then record ALLOC02 applying it to this invoice. After that allocation, recorded amount owed is R60.00, advance held is zero and total cash received remains R30.00. The intermediate table row before allocation deliberately leaves the deposit separate until matched. Day 6 receipt R02 of R60.00 settles the balance. Total cash collected is R90.00, not R120.00. Real deposits, cancellations, refund terms and tax timing require the actual agreement and local bookkeeping guidance; this pack invents none.

practice.title: Dispute demonstration P03
practice.text: Invoice D03-I03 is R200.00; R03-A confirms R120.00 received. Q03 records that the customer questions R40.00. Keep the issue and evidence visible. Merely entering that question does not turn the R80.00 recorded balance into zero or establish that the disputed amount is legally owed. Investigate the delivery, price and agreement. For this synthetic case only, ADJ03 is a separately documented, approved R20.00 reduction. Retain the original invoice and adjustment trail. The resulting recorded balance is R60.00. Receipt R03-B of R60.00 settles it. This is a bookkeeping exercise, not advice to demand a disputed amount or authority to create a tax credit note in the app.

practice.title: Unmatched receipt P04
practice.text: BANK04 proves R25.00 arrived, but no buyer or invoice has been identified. Cash received is R25.00; it stays unmatched. Do not select a convenient unpaid invoice or call it produce sales without evidence. Check the reference and appropriate source safely. If unresolved, retain that status for review.

practice.title: Overpayment P05
practice.text: Invoice D05-I05 is R50.00; R05 proves receipt of R60.00. Only R50.00 settles that invoice. Keep the extra R10.00 as an unresolved customer credit; it is not extra produce revenue or automatically a tip. Confirm an appropriate agreed treatment and its evidence. This exercise performs no refund, future-sale allocation or financial transfer.

practice.title: Guided practice
practice.text: Build a separate customer schedule with original invoice reference, dated receipt references, approved adjustments, allocations and the remaining recorded balance. Keep advance deposits, unknown receipts and customer credits visible. Do not combine unrelated customers' credits and debts into one misleading net figure. In these cases, original invoice less approved reductions minus allocated receipts gives the remaining balance, with any excess shown as customer credit. The model excludes fees, tax and other arrangements.

practice.title: Independent attempt
practice.text: Invoice R150.00, received R50.00. The buyer questions R30.00; no change has been approved. State the recorded balance and label the unresolved question. Then an evidenced R10.00 reduction is approved: recalculate. In a separate case, invoice R35.00 and receipt R40.00: identify the credit. Explain why the app's paid-in-full control cannot represent the first part-payment history or the credit ledger.

practice.title: Feedback and field task
practice.text: If allocation creates cash, reuse the same receipt card rather than introducing another coin. If a dispute automatically changes the invoice, ask for the approved adjustment source and keep the question separate. If overpayment increases sales, return to the delivered amount. Prepare a blank customer schedule and use an invented new case or redacted approved records. Identify the next evidence needed to resolve one item; do not expose customer details or contact anyone as an automatic course action.

shared.title: Prepare the session
shared.text:
Bring paper cards for orders, delivery, invoices and receipts; counters; a calculator; and two envelopes marked “customer owes” and “money received”. Let learners point, sort, explain aloud or ask a partner to write. Keep real customer names, account numbers and private receipts out of group discussion. The app tour uses sample records; these classroom amounts must not be entered in a learner's real farm.

Every amount and numbered day below is an **invented classroom input**. Each P case begins separately with no opening invoice, cash receipt, deposit or credit. The cases contain no tax, discounts, payment fees, refunds or costs unless an event explicitly states an adjustment. They therefore establish neither full profit nor a compliant tax invoice. A single invoice covers each completed delivery in these simplified cases. Real contract terms, tax treatment and disputed rights require appropriate review.
