units.title: Equipment, borrowing and reserves
units.summary: Compare equipment options, understand commitments and plan reserves.

lessons.title: Compare buying, hiring and sharing
lessons.outcome: Compare the same service need, identify cash tied up before use, retain missing information, and explain why a low purchase contribution does not prove a tool will be available.
lessons.reading: Start with the work you need done and the dates. Ask what each offer includes. Buying, hiring and sharing move money at different times. A deposit may come back later, but you still need it before use. Keep the value of a tool you still own separate from cash in your hand. Check who can use a shared tool, when it is available and who pays for damage or repairs.

practice.title: Demonstration
practice.text:
The practice need is the same suitable tool service on Days 2, 10 and 20 within a 30-day horizon. Opening available cash is R500.00. Suitability, safe operation and access for BUY and HIRE are assumed confirmed solely to isolate the money exercise. SHARE has an unconfirmed Day 10 booking. No other receipts are supplied.

BUY pays R900.00 on Day 1, R60.00 for operating inputs on Day 10 and R40.00 for maintenance on Day 20. Total payments are R1,000.00. The plan is already R400.00 short on Day 1 and ends R500.00 short. It cannot be funded from the stated R500.00. The buyer would retain an asset, but its remaining value and useful life are unknown. Do not call the whole purchase an established 30-day cost of using up the tool, or assume the retained asset is worth zero. A future sale of that asset is not cash until its price, costs and date are evidenced.

HIRE pays R210.00 for all three uses, R60.00 transport and R150.00 refundable security on Day 1. These are three parts of one offer, not three separate R210.00 service fees. The exercise says operating and maintenance service costs are included, no other charges apply, and the R150.00 deposit is returned in full on Day 30. Cash needed first is R420.00, leaving R80.00. After the refund, net cash paid is R270.00 and closing cash is R230.00. A R270.00 net figure does not mean the farmer could start with only R270.00. The refund returns the farmer's money; it is not a produce sale.

SHARE pays R300.00 towards ownership on Day 1, R30.00 operating contribution on Day 10 and R20.00 maintenance contribution on Day 20. The conditional cash plan uses R350.00 and closes at R150.00. The retained share value is unknown. The unconfirmed booking means this offer has not yet been shown to meet the same need. A favourable cash total cannot resolve that availability problem.

practice.title: Guided comparison
practice.text: Lay out all source cards by date, keeping the refundable deposit distinct. Check the included operator, transport, fuel or other operating inputs, cleaning, repair, storage, return terms, insurance and downtime arrangements in an actual offer. In this synthetic comparison the stated package assumptions are complete for the shown cash movements; they do not establish complete economic costs. None of the three totals proves full profitability or a lifetime winner.

practice.title: Independent attempt
practice.text: A different hire costs R80.00, plus a R50.00 security deposit returned fully later. Find the amount needed before hire and net cash paid after refund. Then remove the refund agreement: which conclusion is no longer established? For a shared tool, name the missing agreement if two members need the same slot.

practice.title: Feedback and field task
practice.text: If the deposit is ignored, place the payment before the first use and its refund after the last use. If an unknown asset value becomes zero, replace it with a precise evidence request. If sharing is called cheapest without availability, ask how the required Day 10 work happens. Obtain a dated redacted quote or a list of questions for a supplier/group. Record the job, dates, inclusions, ownership and access terms. Do not buy, borrow or sign anything as an automatic lesson activity.

practice.title: App connection
practice.text: Use the [expense guide](https://imbewufield.vercel.app/student/guides/expenses) for supported actual cost entries and receipt evidence. Keep the comparison, deposit schedule and asset/share record separately. The app's cost tag is not a complete asset register, depreciation calculation or tool-booking system. Do not enter every proposed offer as an actual expense or create an invented produce sale for a deposit refund.

lessons.title: Read the whole borrowing commitment
lessons.outcome: Reconcile money received, fees, principal and repayment dates; recognise an incomplete quote; and connect a proposed repayment to a dated cash plan without claiming that arithmetic alone proves affordability.
lessons.reading: The amount borrowed is not the amount you may have left to spend. Read the fees and when they are paid. Each instalment may contain repayment of the amount borrowed, interest and other charges. If a charge is already included, do not add it again. Keep the dates. A smaller-looking instalment is not enough information to choose a loan.

practice.title: Source-reading demonstration
practice.text: Use the current [NCR quotation form](https://www.ncr.org.za/index.php/act/list-of-forms/category/123-english?download=480:english) to locate fields, not to manufacture a contract. Identify the advance, deposit if applicable, instalment count/frequency, interest information, fees, required and optional insurance, security and repayment arrangements. Ask a qualified local adviser about applicability and unclear terms. Do not infer a legal limit or a right from this lesson. No form is signed.

practice.title: Worked SEPARATE case
practice.text:
In this original model, R600.00 principal is advanced on 1 January 2027 and credited in full. A R30.00 fee is paid separately that day, leaving R570.00 from the advance available for the intended purpose. The quoted schedule has three principal payments of R200.00. Interest components are R12.00, R8.00 and R4.00. Each instalment also includes R6.00 service and R4.00 required insurance. No optional insurance or other charges are assumed in this model. These are supplied charge amounts, not an interest calculation or a statement that such terms comply with law.

The payments due are R222.00 on 31 January, R218.00 on 28 February and R214.00 on 31 March. Their total is R654.00. With the separate R30.00 fee, total outflow is R684.00 against the R600.00 gross advance. Specified financing charges are R84.00: interest R24.00, service R18.00, insurance R12.00 and the initial fee R30.00. Repaying R600.00 principal is not an additional R600.00 interest expense or produce sale. Remaining principal is R400.00, R200.00 and zero after the three scheduled payments. That number excludes future charges; label it remaining principal, not a complete early-settlement quote.

practice.title: WITHHELD case
practice.text: Now keep the same principal, fee and repayment schedule, but the provider withholds the R30.00 fee once before paying out R570.00. Do not subtract it again from the R570.00 actually credited. The scheduled R654.00 outflow less R570.00 received still gives R84.00 financing charges. The apparent bank receipt differs, but these two cases have the same net initial funds and specified total charges. A fee added to the loan principal would be a different arrangement and needs its own supplied schedule; it is not silently substituted here.

practice.title: UNKNOWN case
practice.text: A different practice quote shows principal R600.00, a separate R30.00 fee, three R200.00 principal components and R10.00 interest per instalment, with no service fee. Required insurance applies but its amount is missing. Each full instalment, the full repayment total and total financing charges remain unknown. The displayed remaining principal assumes the specified principal payments are made; it does not confirm payment or full settlement when charges are unresolved. Do not set missing insurance to zero and advertise this as a cheaper loan. Obtain the required amount, its payment timing and a corrected complete schedule.

practice.title: Guided practice
practice.text: Separate the principal and charges in each dated row. Match the total to the document rather than adding an included service fee twice. Link each proposed due date to a cash forecast that includes other obligations. Check the actual purpose, disbursement timing, rate basis, variable-rate exposure where applicable, fees, insurance, collateral and consequences of default with suitable help. This practice pack has no complete business-income forecast, household commitments or lender assessment, so it cannot certify affordability or recommend borrowing.

practice.title: Independent attempt
practice.text: A separate payment consists of R100.00 principal, R10.00 interest and R2.00 service already included in the instalment. Calculate that instalment. A learner adds the service again: explain the error. Then give an offer with missing compulsory insurance and ask what prevents a complete comparison.

practice.title: Feedback and field task
practice.text: If loan receipts become sales revenue, link the money to its repayment obligation. If a fee is charged twice, trace whether it was withheld, paid separately or already included. If the learner chooses the unknown offer by its apparent total, restore the missing field. Collect a blank or approved redacted quote and list questions. Keep original terms and dates. Do not apply for credit, choose a lender, enter private identity details or transfer money as a lesson exercise.

practice.title: App connection
practice.text: The current My Records summaries and lender record export are not this repayment schedule, a credit assessment or an automatic affordability decision. Keep the complete schedule and supporting evidence separately. F4 supplies dated cash planning; F7 will address statement boundaries. Do not force a loan advance into a produce sale or imply the app distinguishes principal and finance charges automatically.

lessons.title: Set money aside and test a shock
lessons.outcome: Distinguish a reserve allocation from money received or spent, retain restricted/earmarked funds in the correct scope, and identify a later cash gap after an unexpected repair.
lessons.reading: Setting money aside gives it a job. It does not create more money. If you move it between two accounts you own, the total is unchanged unless there is a fee. When you pay someone else for a repair, money leaves. Keep the amount still set aside separate from money for daily work. A reserve target is a plan, not an account balance.

practice.title: Demonstration
practice.text:
Start this separate case with R800.00 total owned cash: R600.00 for daily work and R200.00 earmarked. Both are inside the same scope, available to the owner, with no transfer fees or legal restrictions supplied. Earmarking is a management allocation; real contractual restrictions must be checked separately. A target of R500.00 is an invented goal for the exercise, not a recommended reserve size.

On Day 5 allocate R100.00 from daily work to the reserve. Daily work becomes R500.00 and reserve R300.00; total remains R800.00. On Day 10 pay a R120.00 maintenance bill from the reserve: reserve R180.00 and total R680.00. On Day 15 an evidenced R80.00 operating receipt arrives: daily work R580.00, reserve R180.00, total R760.00. Its source belongs with the receipt; the amount alone does not establish profit. On Day 25 a specified R550.00 essential bill leaves daily work R30.00 and reserve R180.00, total R210.00. The reserve is R320.00 below the invented R500.00 target.

Keep D01, a separate R50.00 non-cash equipment-use estimate, out of these cash movements. It neither pays for replacement nor moves money into the bank. Keep the unapproved R300.00 funding application G01 out too. A proposal is not money received. This lesson does not prescribe depreciation or its tax treatment.

practice.title: SHOCK case
practice.text: Return to the original opening position and insert a R250.00 repair on Day 20. After Day 15 only R180.00 is reserved. Using that plus R70.00 from daily work is a proposed change of plan, not additional income. Total falls from R760.00 to R510.00, with reserve zero. The later R550.00 essential bill would then produce a R40.00 shortage. Stop and investigate a feasible response before that bill is due. Do not silently clip the negative answer to zero or treat an unapproved application as the missing R40.00.

practice.title: Guided discussion
practice.text: If the earmarked amount were legally restricted or unavailable, permission/access would be a separate constraint; this exercise assumes none. A response may require revising timing by agreement, obtaining reliable repair alternatives or reassessing the work and its consequences. Do not automatically cancel essential maintenance, divert protected funds or borrow. Recalculate the resulting dates and amounts from actual evidence. A reserve target must be grounded in the farmer's circumstances, not a universal percentage.

practice.title: Independent attempt
practice.text: Start a new case with R400.00 total and no reserve. Earmark R90.00. Then pay R20.00 from that reserve. State total cash after the allocation and after the external payment, including what remains reserved. Explain why a non-cash cost estimate cannot pay the next repair.

practice.title: Feedback and field task
practice.text: If allocation reduces total money, physically move counters between the two envelopes without removing any. For an external payment, remove its counters once. If the later shortage disappears, replay the repair before the essential bill. Prepare a redacted list of maintenance needs, their evidence, likely payment dates, funds genuinely available and unresolved costs. Keep the target, actual balance and obligations distinct. No private bank balance must be shared with the class.

practice.title: App connection
practice.text: Keep reserve allocation and replacement planning in the workbook unless a supported ledger represents them faithfully. Use the expense companion for actual recorded costs, with original receipt evidence. The app chart does not establish your unrestricted bank balance, asset value or depreciation provision.

shared.title: Prepare the session
shared.text:
Bring three cards marked Buy, Hire and Share, counters, a calculator and two envelopes marked Daily work and Set aside. Read one source card at a time. Learners may point, sort, explain aloud or ask a partner to write. Keep private financial details out of group work. Use approved redacted documents only when people agree to discuss them.

Every rand amount, day, date, fee and schedule here is **invented for arithmetic practice**. None is a local quote, normal price, legal maximum, interest-rate recommendation or offer of credit. The tool is deliberately unspecified. No crop, yield, machine capacity or instruction to perform a farming operation is supplied. Each exercise starts separately; do not carry cash or debt from another case. Full profit remains unknown.

A negative cash projection is an unfunded shortage, not spendable money or an approved overdraft. Continuing the calculation shows a proposed plan's problem; it does not prove the intervening payments can be made. Real affordability needs the full household/farm commitments and income evidence, which this unit does not supply.

| SHOCK/A01 | 5 | R500.00 | R300.00 | R800.00 |
| SHOCK/M01 | 10 | R500.00 | R180.00 | R680.00 |
| SHOCK/R01 | 15 | R580.00 | R180.00 | R760.00 |
| SHOCK/X01 | 20 | R510.00 | R0.00 | R510.00 |

Independent: R130.00 needed before hire; R80.00 net after refund; R112.00 instalment including its service fee; R400.00 total after allocation; R380.00 after the payment, including R70.00 still reserved.

The independent deposit refund depends on its stated full-return assumption. Remove that agreement and net cash paid is unresolved. In the borrowing examples, the supplied principal is repaid exactly; an actual outstanding account, early settlement or changing interest needs its own evidence. BASE closes with R180.00 reserved, R320.00 below target. SHOCK has zero reserved and a projected R40.00 cash shortage after the essential bill; no source of funding has been supplied.

units.title: Read results and prepare reliable records
units.summary: Separate cash, period result and financial position; prepare reliable records.

lessons.title: Three views of one business
lessons.outcome: Point to the record that answers each question: what cash moved during a period; what income and costs belong to that period; and what the business owns and owes at a date. Explain why one total cannot answer all three.
lessons.reading: Start by saying which business and which dates you mean. Our stall starts with money, stock, equipment and amounts owed. A cash summary follows money received and paid. A profit-and-loss view follows the period's income and costs. A balance sheet shows the position on a date: assets, liabilities and what remains for the owner. The views are connected, but their totals need not match. Borrowed money increases cash and debt. It does not become a sale. A customer can owe us for goods already delivered. That sale can be recorded before the money reaches us.

practice.title: Demonstration
practice.text:
Lay out three spaces: Cash, Period result, Position. Show R01. Move R200 from “customer owes” to “cash”; do not add a January sale. Show S01: add R900 to sales and the customer balance; move R350 of stock into goods cost. Cash stays R950 after P01. The running result is R550 before later costs and checks. Then R02 moves R600 from the customer balance into cash. Sales remain R900; R300 remains owed. This model assumes the delivery and accepted invoice establish that sale; an order or an unfulfilled promise alone would not be the same evidence.

Continue with L01: cash and debt both rise R500, while the result stays unchanged. Use the interactive aid one card at a time. Invite the learner to predict which of the three views changes before advancing. Early cards show a running result from the evidence processed so far, not a completed month's profit.

practice.title: Guided practice
practice.text: Sort P02, E01, L02 and H01. For each, say what cash leaves and whether the supplied case records a period cost. P02 settles a supplier balance. E01 changes cash into equipment. L02 has two parts: principal reduces debt; the R10 interest is a period cost. H01 reduces cash and the owner's equity; it is not a business expense here. Do not generalise this personal withdrawal into a rule about salaries in every business form.

practice.title: Worked January summaries, after all checks
practice.text:
Cash receipts total R1300: R200 old balance + R600 current receipt + R500 borrowing. Payments total R1190. Opening R1000 + R1300 − R1190 = closing cash R1110, an increase of R110. February's R300 receipt is excluded. This is a cash summary; it is not a standards-compliant statement of cash flows with all classifications and disclosures.

Sales R900 less goods supplied R350, interest R10, transport R80, utilities R60, stock loss R50 and depreciation R60 gives **R290 result before tax in this model**. No tax amount is inferred. Closing assets are cash R1110 + customers owing R300 + stock R300 + equipment R840 + prepayment R120 = R2670. Liabilities are supplier/service balances R330 + loan R400 = R730. Equity is R1940. Check R2670 = R730 + R1940, and R1800 opening equity + R290 result − R150 personal withdrawal = R1940.

practice.title: Independent attempt
practice.text: Begin another case: cash R400 and resale stock R120, no debts. Deliver the entire stock for a R300 credit sale, then receive R200 of that sale. Ask for cash, the customer balance, remaining stock, result and total assets. Answer: R600 cash, R100 owed, no stock remaining, R180 result and R700 assets. The opening equity R520 plus the R180 result also equals R700. The R200 receipt must not be counted as another sale.

practice.title: Corrective feedback
practice.text: If a learner calls R110 January profit, ask which cash movements were borrowing, equipment or a household withdrawal and which period costs had no January payment. If they add a receipt to sales twice, physically join the invoice and receipt with the same reference, then repeat the fresh example.

practice.title: Field task and app connection
practice.text: Choose one redacted recorded sale and its evidence. Say which part is a sale, receipt or unpaid amount. Read the Sales and Invoice app companions before changing an entry. Charts presents recorded information; it does not create this complete position, stock valuation or loan ledger. Keep these practice figures outside actual My Records.

lessons.title: Close the period without hiding gaps
lessons.outcome: Separate event, document and payment dates. Explain why stock, equipment, unpaid costs and future services matter at the period boundary. Keep an unsupported value unknown.
lessons.reading: A document can arrive after the work. Payment can happen before or after the service. Keep those dates together. At the end of our month, ask what was delivered, used, owed and still available. A bank line alone cannot answer every question. Check the stock and equipment records too. When evidence is missing, write what you still need. Do not enter zero just to finish a total.

practice.title: Demonstration
practice.text:
Place A01 across the January–February boundary. Work was completed in January at the agreed R80 charge. The invoice is dated February and the amount is unpaid at January end. Under this model, January includes the R80 cost and liability, while January cash does not change. Retain both documents and dates. Now place F01: cash leaves in January, but the whole storage service is for February. January includes a R120 prepayment asset, not a January storage cost. A real contract may need different treatment; this case supplies the timing and rights explicitly.

Show the stock bridge: opening R300 + purchases R400 − goods supplied R350 = R350 before the closing check. C01 supports a R50 loss and R300 remaining. This is a reviewed reconciliation, not an instruction to label every unexplained difference as theft or spoilage. Ask for evidence before choosing a cause or accounting treatment. Show the equipment bridge: opening R600 + purchase R300 − supplied period depreciation R60 = R840. The charge spreads cost in this model but is not a new payment and is not a tax allowance.

practice.title: Guided practice
practice.text: Run the missing-stock case. Withhold C01 entirely. The book shows R350 before review, but the physical count, valuation and adjustment are unknown. Cash R1110, customer balances R300, equipment R840, prepayment R120, payables R330 and loan R400 still have supplied support. **Adjusted stock, complete period result, total assets and equity are unknown.** Do not reuse R300 from the complete case after its evidence has been removed. Ask the learner to identify the precise document that would allow a reliable update.

practice.title: Independent attempt
practice.text: New case: start with cash R200 and no other balance. Pay R90 for a service supplied wholly next month, with the right unused at this month's end. Cash becomes R110; the prepayment is R90; the period result is R0; total assets remain R200. If the service period is missing from the document, the R90 payment is known but that classification is not established. Request the agreement and service dates rather than assuming all of it is a current expense.

practice.title: Corrective feedback
practice.text: If the learner puts A01 into February only because of the invoice date, point to the January service evidence. If they call every purchase an expense, compare stock still held, equipment and a service already used. If they equate a balanced equation with accurate accounts, show that a wrong classification can still balance: evidence and period checks are needed too.

practice.title: Field task and app connection
practice.text: Assemble a small period-end folder: opening balances, sales and deliveries, receipts, supplier bills, payments, stock evidence, equipment schedule, debt schedule and unresolved questions. Keep original references and dates. An export from the app is one input to that folder. Do not invent stock, depreciation or loan entries in a crop-sale form to force a chart to match this exercise.

lessons.title: Prepare records and ask the right tax questions
lessons.outcome: Assemble an evidence pack and find the appropriate current official guidance. Distinguish a readable app invoice from a verified compliant tax invoice. State what remains unconfirmed without guessing a tax rate, deadline or registration outcome.
lessons.reading: Keep the story behind a number. Who supplied what? When did it happen? Which document supports it? Which money movement belongs with it? Keep records organised and safe. Tax and record duties depend on the business and its circumstances. Use current SARS guidance and suitable help. A saved invoice, tax-reference field or app export cannot confirm all those duties for you.

practice.title: Demonstration
practice.text:
Use an invented pack, not a learner's private identifiers. Put an opening balance list, source documents, account statements, stock check, equipment and debt schedules, and unresolved items behind a one-page index. Give each a reference and period. Reconcile the index against the summaries. Mark missing items visibly. Keep actuals separate from forecasts. Do not ask learners to send private financial documents to a public class or to an unverified adviser.

Open the current official SARS pages in the source notes. Show how to record the page title, URL, date checked and the exact question. For example: which business form and registrations apply; what records are required; which retention conditions apply; whether an invoice has the required particulars for the relevant supply; and whether electronic storage arrangements meet the applicable requirements. This is an evidence-finding exercise, not a conclusion that a particular learner must register or can discard records. Retain source documents while questions remain unresolved. Do not teach a universal destruction date from a short web table.

practice.title: Guided practice
practice.text:
Discuss four cards:

1. “The app printed a VAT number, so this is a valid tax invoice.” **Not established.** A field or title alone does not establish registration, supply treatment or all required particulars. Inspect the document with the applicable current guidance.
2. “I did not need to submit a return, so no records are needed.” **Not established.** Do not infer all record duties from that fact. Ask about the applicable requirements and any continuing audit, dispute or other obligation.
3. “My export is a complete set of accounts and guarantees a loan.” **Not established.** Check it against the other evidence. An export does not establish completeness, creditworthiness or approval.
4. “A missing stock value should be zero.” **Incorrect.** Request the count, valuation and reconciliation. Do not disguise missing information as a measured result.

practice.title: Independent attempt
practice.text: Give an invoice and cash export with no stock check, unpaid-customer list or equipment schedule. Ask the learner to prepare an index of supplied and missing evidence, name one specific question for a bookkeeper, and record a current SARS source to consult for one compliance question. Accept an oral explanation or a card sort. A satisfactory answer separates known documents from missing ones and does not claim the export proves profit, complete accounts or tax compliance. The answer must be based on the supplied pack, not private records.

practice.title: Corrective feedback
practice.text: If the learner asks for “the tax number that makes everything correct,” return to the supply, business status, document and current rules. If they try to fill gaps with plausible figures, ask them to label the gap and identify who or what can resolve it. Repeat with a different missing document.

practice.title: Field task and app connection
practice.text: Reopen the appropriate saved invoice and inspect its details without sending it. Use the invoice companion and, when available, the export companion. Prepare a private evidence index and questions for appropriate local help. Keep a readable copy and recovery plan for needed records. Do not assume a device-local document has synchronised to another device, or that a course completion badge certifies the business's accounts.

shared.title: Shared practice case
shared.text:
A small market stall buys finished goods for resale. It is a separate exercise within the farm-business pathway, not a valuation of growing crops, animals, home-grown harvests or an entire homestead. All amounts and dates are invented. The period is 1–31 January 2027. Values below are supplied carrying amounts for the exercise; they are not market quotations. No VAT or income-tax calculation is included. Equipment classification, depreciation and stock-loss treatment are supplied assumptions, not policies to copy into real accounts.

At opening: cash R1000; customers owe R200; resale stock R300; equipment R600. The business owes suppliers R300 and has no loan. Total assets R2100 less liabilities R300 leaves opening equity R1800. Equity is the owner's residual interest, not a second cash account. There are no other opening balances in this bounded model.

| Ref | Event date | Original source card |
| --- | --- | --- |
| R01 | 5 Jan | Collect R200 from the opening customer balance. This older sale is not January revenue. |
| P01 | 8 Jan | Receive resale goods costing R400. Pay R250; R150 remains owed. |
| S01 | 10 Jan | Deliver an accepted credit sale of R900. Goods supplied have carrying cost R350. No receipt yet. |
| R02 | 15 Jan | Receive R600 toward S01. Link the receipt to that sale. |
| P02 | 16 Jan | Pay R200 against amounts already owed to suppliers. |
| E01 | 20 Jan | Pay R300 for a lasting tool. It qualifies as equipment in this exercise. |
| L01 | 21 Jan | Receive a R500 loan with a matching obligation. No initial fee here. |
| L02 | 24 Jan | Pay R110: R100 loan principal and R10 January interest. |
| H01 | 26 Jan | Owner takes R150 for personal use. No wage or business service is supplied. |
| A01 | 28 Jan | January transport service completed, agreed charge R80, unpaid. Invoice arrives 2 February; a signed January work record supports the amount and period. |
| F01 | 29 Jan | Pay R120 for storage supplied wholly in February. None of that service is used by 31 January. |
| U01 | 31 Jan | Pay R60 utility cost relating wholly to January. |
| C01 | 31 Jan | Approved count, valuation and reconciliation confirm closing resale stock R300 and a R50 stock loss. |
| D01 | 31 Jan | Supplied reviewed schedule gives R60 January depreciation across the equipment. It is not an extra cash payment. |
| X01 | 5 Feb | Receive the remaining R300 of S01. This is outside January cash. |

units.title: Plan, compare and improve the business
units.summary: Test market evidence, write a checkable plan and review a season.

lessons.title: Choose an enterprise from evidence
lessons.outcome: Compare two options using demand evidence, the same period, available resources and dated cash needs; explain a missing assumption before choosing a next action.
lessons.reading: Start with a buyer and a task you can deliver. What does the buyer need? How much, in which unit, at what quality, and by when? Interest is not an order. A high sales total does not tell you what you will keep or whether you can pay the earlier bills. Put the alternatives beside each other. Keep the missing evidence visible.

practice.title: Observe and sort
practice.text: Lay out M-A and M-B. Ask the learner to point to a documented statement, a planning assumption and an unanswered question. M-A is an enquiry about up to 40 kg at R12 per kg, subject to quality and confirmation. The forecast assumes the full quantity sells and the money arrives on 30 January. M-B expresses interest in baskets at R30 each, but confirms no quantity. The forecast's 20 items is an assumption, not a completed market survey or agreed order. Neither document proves a secure market. Ask about grade, acceptance, quantities, delivery costs, payment terms, repeat demand and alternative buyers. Keep a date and source beside each answer.

practice.title: Demonstration
practice.text:
For January, Plan A forecasts sales of R480 and operating payments of R280. Plan B forecasts R600 and operating payments of R480. Their included cash surpluses are R200 and R120 respectively, assuming all forecast sales are paid within the period. These are not full profits: closing stock, equipment use, overheads and unpaid work are not completely supplied. Do not treat the omitted costs as zero. Do not compare R12 per kg with R30 per item as though the larger number identifies the better enterprise.

Each alternative starts with R300. A's quoted payments leave R120 on 5 January, R80 on 10 January and R20 on 20 January. The assumed R480 payment on 30 January brings its closing projection to R500. B's payments leave R20, then an unfunded -R120, then -R180; its assumed receipt brings the closing projection to R420. A positive closing forecast does not make those earlier B payments fundable. The negative amounts are projected gaps, not an assertion that a physical cash tin held negative notes or that an overdraft was approved.

The supplied work plan allows eight owner hours. A requires six; B requires ten in addition to its paid helper. B has a two-hour owner-time gap. Those are exercise capacities, not recommended work rates. A's apparent fit does not establish that a real farm has sufficient land, water, skills, labour or permissions. Check each real constraint separately using suitable local evidence.

practice.title: Guided practice
practice.text: Sort each source into “supports this fact”, “assumption to test” or “missing”. Show the first projected shortage on the dated cash line. Ask the learner to justify a next step, not announce a universal winning enterprise. A defensible answer is to investigate A further while confirming buyer terms, the complete costs and deliverability. Another is to revise B's scope and obtain evidence for labour and cash arrangements before any commitment. “B wins because R600 is bigger” fails. “A is guaranteed profitable” also fails.

practice.title: Independent attempt
practice.text: Hide the demonstration. Give the separate items case: planned ten items at R15 each, R60 payments and R80 opening cash. Ask for sales and closing cash, then ask whether these alone prove profit. Next remove the buyer's confirmed quantity from a fresh enquiry. The learner must name a market question rather than fill the blank with ten. Finally show kg beside items: ask which measures can be compared and which cannot be added directly.

practice.title: Feedback
practice.text: If sales become profit, put the excluded-cost card beside the surplus. If January's final cash hides the earlier gap, replay B one bill at a time. If the learner calls an enquiry an order, point to its conditional wording. Use a new example after correction; do not give a pass for repeating the model's answer.

practice.title: Field task and app connection
practice.text: Prepare a small market enquiry sheet with product, unit, quality, quantity, collection/delivery, date and payment terms. Record who supplied information and permission to keep it; use redacted copies in class. Use the mapping guide to identify the correct site and distinguish beds from a whole parcel. A place pin does not prove productive area or land rights. Keep these enterprise forecasts in the workbook; My Records is for supported actual entries.

lessons.title: Turn the idea into a checkable plan
lessons.outcome: Present a connected plan whose claims lead back to evidence, show timing and constraints, and distinguish an unapproved funding request from available cash.
lessons.reading: A useful plan lets another person follow your reasoning. Say what you intend to sell, why a buyer may want it, and what you need to deliver it. Show the work and payments in order. Keep estimates separate from records. If a number or permission is missing, name it and say how you will check it. A neat document cannot turn an application into money.

practice.title: Demonstration pack
practice.text:
Build eight short sections: purpose and chosen activity; market evidence; site and resource access; work and delivery sequence; cost assumptions; dated cash forecast; risks and responses; review actions. Give every significant figure a reference, date, unit, scope and status. Mark a quotation as a quotation, an enquiry as an enquiry and an actual payment as a record. Keep an original plan version and a date for revisions. Explain the business in plain language before presenting the numbers.

For A, connect the three quote cards to the cash line and its assumed buyer payment. Keep B as a genuine alternative, with its hours and earlier cash gap visible. Do not combine the two R300 opening balances. A funding application F-ASK for R180 has no approval, terms or disbursement date. It does not fill B's gap. Even an approval may have conditions and timing to check; this lesson gives no approval or borrowing recommendation. F6 supplies questions for reading actual finance terms.

practice.title: Test timing
practice.text:
Move A's entire assumed R480 receipt to 5 February, retaining January's cost dates. January now has no buyer receipt and ends at R20. The projected sale remains R480; payment timing changed, not the quantity or price. The amount remains expected from the buyer at the window's end under this scenario. This is a January horizon, not a full next-season plan: later bills and obligations still need their own dated rows. A real forecast should cover the relevant operating cycle and commitments, rather than copying this short exercise horizon blindly.

A response must be specific and checked. For example, ask the buyer to confirm terms, then record any actual agreement and recalculate; obtain a genuine alternative transport quote; reconsider the proposed quantity against capacity. Do not assume a deposit, delay a supplier's bill without agreement, cut necessary care or insert hoped-for funding as certain income. Explain the effects on quality, workload, household needs and others before adopting a change.

practice.title: Guided practice
practice.text: Give one learner the proposed plan and another the evidence cards. For each claim ask “which record supports it?” Put missing demand confirmation, full cost treatment and site/resource evidence into an action register with an owner and review date. The model's proposed 10 February 2027 review is a classroom date, not a universal planning interval. Ask what could make the plan wrong and what observation would trigger reconsideration. Keep a funding pack's requested information separate from what the class currently knows.

practice.title: Independent attempt
practice.text: A learner submits a polished map, a screenshot of R420 closing projected cash and the R180 application. Explain why these do not prove land rights, earlier liquidity, profitability or funding approval. Ask for the dated B payments and the missing work-hour arrangement. Then give A's delayed receipt case without the answer and ask the learner to build January cash. They must leave the February receipt outside January.

practice.title: Feedback
practice.text: If a forecast is relabelled as actual, return to the source status. If an application pays the bill in the model, remove it and restore the gap. If a claim rests on the map's appearance, ask for the appropriate underlying agreement, measurement or record. A legitimate answer may be “not ready to commit; obtain this evidence”. It is not a failure to preserve uncertainty.

practice.title: Field task and app connection
practice.text: Build a redacted practice plan and a short evidence index. Use the live mapping, invoice and Charts guides for supported tasks. A record export or “Records for a lender” summary is supporting material, not a full application, a title document, complete financial statements or an eligibility decision. Check the current requirements with the relevant organisation when preparing a real pack. Keep private documents secure; this lesson sends nothing to a lender or buyer.

lessons.title: Review the season without rewriting its history
lessons.outcome: Reconcile an original forecast with actual records, separate quantity, price, collection and cost differences, preserve a missing value, and set a justified next action.
lessons.reading: Keep the plan you started with. Put the actual records beside it for the same period and units. What sold? What money arrived? What was paid? Which amounts are still owed? Explain each difference with evidence before saying why it happened. Then make the next plan. Changing the old plan to match the result hides what you learned.

practice.title: Demonstration
practice.text:
Actual A has 36 kg delivered at R11 per kg on 25 January, an invoice for R396. R300 arrives on 30 January, leaving R96 owed at 31 January. The remaining R96 arrives on 5 February; it is not January cash. Actual payments are purchase R180, packaging R50 and transport R80, totalling R310. An evidenced R20 owner contribution arrives on 15 January from outside this business cash scope. It is not a sale or loan. Starting with R300, the actual cash sequence is R120, R70, R90, R10 and R310. ACT-C1 reconciles the final R310 to the cash count and statement evidence. This complete model has no unfunded actual negative balance.

The closing forecast was R500; checked actual closing cash is R310, a R190 decrease against that forecast. Do not call this R190 a business loss. The sales-value difference is R84, and neither difference establishes full profit. Use the visual bridge in this stated order:

- Quantity effect: (36 - 40) kg at the planned R12 per kg = -R48.
- Price effect: 36 actual kg at (R11 - R12) per kg = -R36.
- Unpaid January balance: -R96 of the invoiced amount is not yet received.
- Purchase payment difference: R180 versus R180, no change.
- Packaging payment difference: R50 versus R40 reduces cash by R10.
- Transport payment difference: R80 versus R60 reduces cash by R20.
- Owner contribution adds R20 cash, not sales.

R500 - R48 - R36 - R96 - R10 - R20 + R20 = R310. The quantity and price effects sum to the R84 sales difference. This decomposition values the quantity change at planned price and the price change at actual quantity; different valid ordering allocates the interaction differently. It is arithmetic attribution, not proof of cause. The records do not say why fewer kilos sold or why the price changed. Do not invent crop failure, poor effort, buyer misconduct or weather as the explanation. Investigate using appropriate evidence.

practice.title: Guided practice
practice.text: Trace every bridge step back to its source. Ask why the invoice and its two receipts are not three sales, and why the owner contribution does not increase product revenue. Keep January and February windows visible. If a learner changes the plan quantity to 36, restore the original 40 before comparing. Ask for a reasoned next action such as confirming quality/demand and payment terms, checking current quotes, and fitting work to available hours. The actual R11 and 36 kg inform an enquiry; they do not guarantee next month's price or sales.

practice.title: Missing-evidence case
practice.text: Hide the amount on ACT-P2 and remove ACT-C1's closing reconciliation. Packaging was paid but its amount is unavailable. Full payments, closing cash, the cash difference and deepest gap now remain unknown. Sales of R396 and the January customer balance of R96 stay supported. Do not use the other case's R310 closing figure to reconstruct the missing amount. With a separate trustworthy closing reconciliation, a discrepancy could be investigated; this case deliberately does not supply one. Keep a request for the receipt and reconciliation open.

practice.title: Independent attempt
practice.text: Return to the separate items case. Plan: ten items at R15, R60 payments, R80 opening. Actual: eight items at R14, R90 received, R70 payments and R20 contributed by the owner; no other movements or opening customer balance. Find actual sales, customer balance, closing cash and the difference from plan. Decompose the sales change with the same order as the demonstration. Then remove the actual cost evidence and ask which answers remain supported. Do not label a missing amount zero.

practice.title: Feedback and assessment
practice.text: The learner must produce R112 sales, R22 still owed and R120 closing cash against the R170 plan, a -R50 cash difference. Sales quantity effect is -R30 and price effect -R8, totalling -R38. Closing bridge: R170 - R30 - R8 - R22 - R10 + R20 = R120. Correct explanations distinguish product sales, money received, owner funds and the period. If a concept is missed, give corrective feedback and a new small source set; do not change the old answer to count it as independent success.

practice.title: Field task and app connection
practice.text: Write a short review with the original assumption, actual evidence, explained difference, unresolved question, next action, responsible person and review date. Use the Charts guide to check each display's time window and cost scope. The app's single paid-in-full date does not reproduce this partial-payment history; keep the settlement schedule separately and do not mark a deposit as full payment. Do not enter invented classroom figures into a real farm's records.

shared.title: Practice setting
shared.text:
Use `f8-practice.json`, the learner workbook and the visual comparison together. All money, dates, quantities and hours are invented classroom inputs. They are not local prices, yields, recommended workloads or farming forecasts. This case concerns a produce-selling activity and a basket-selling activity; it does not model production from land. Keep kilos and items separate. Both are alternatives using the same opening money, not two activities that can each spend it simultaneously. The actual case is an invented record set shown after the plan, not a prediction of what will happen.

Build on F3 cost boundaries, F4 cash timing, F5 payment evidence and F7 complete-account boundaries. Supply counters, source cards, a calculator and writing space. A learner may explain aloud or point while a facilitator records the reasoning. No real buyer details or bank documents are needed.

shared.title: Checked answers
shared.text:
All cash values are within the stated January scope. Plan gaps are unfunded projections. Complete profit stays unknown. The original cases compare currencies over one period, not quantities across unlike units.

| Case | Sales | Buyer receipts | Payments | Closing cash | Lowest cash | Cash gap |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Plan A | R480.00 | R480.00 | R280.00 | R500.00 | R20.00 | R0.00 |
| Plan B | R600.00 | R600.00 | R480.00 | R420.00 | -R180.00 | R180.00 |
| Actual A | R396.00 | R300.00 | R310.00 | R310.00 | R10.00 | R0.00 |

Plan B needs two more owner hours than supplied. Delayed Plan A has R480 projected sales, zero January buyer receipts and R20 January closing cash. Actual A has R96 owed at 31 January. Owner funds R20 are included only in actual cash. Missing-case closing cash and full profit stay unknown.

shared.title: Connected capstone
shared.text:
The learner presents an original/revised plan pair with: one market evidence sheet; a resource and access check; an activity budget with exclusions; dated cash rows; a delivery/invoice/payment trail; a cost evidence index; an actual-versus-plan review; and a next-action register. Use only systems relevant to that learner. A farming plan needs appropriate land, resource and technical evidence beyond this market exercise. The map and app records can support the pack but cannot replace those checks.

Assess whether the learner can detect an unconfirmed buyer assumption, an unfunded early payment, double-counted income, unlike units, an unpaid invoice counted as cash, an owner contribution called sales, an out-of-period receipt, missing costs presented as zero and a forecast presented as actual. Record the evidence of performance, feedback and next practice. Do not claim accounting competence, business viability, accreditation or funding approval from this classroom pack.
